title: Skills Readiness for Network Automation  and AI-Enabled Networking among Emerging IT Professionals in Bangladesh
content: The transition from manually administered networks toward programmable, automated and AI-enabled  networking is not only a technological transformation; it is a workforce-capability problem. This study  examines how emerging IT professionals in Bangladesh translate perceptions of networking  technology value into skills readiness and, ultimately, adoption and career intention. Drawing on the  Technology Acceptance Model, Technology Readiness logic and Human Capital Theory, the study  develops a capability-translation perspective in which perceived usefulness, perceived reliability and  relative advantage stimulate skills readiness, while skills readiness translates into future adoption and  career intention. The Group 9 Cisco master dataset contained 400 numbered records; 15 were  completely blank and 385 complete responses were retained. The analysis combines data screening,  descriptive diagnostics, reliability and validity assessment, multivariate regression, bootstrap  mediation, effect-size analysis, predictive cross-validation and a readiness-gap diagnostic. The results  show a distinctive pattern: perceived usefulness (M = 4.04), relative advantage (M = 3.93), perceived  reliability (M = 3.97) and adoption/career intention (M = 4.02) were comparatively high, whereas skills  readiness was lower (M = 3.60). The paired difference between technology readiness and skills  readiness was 0.224 scale points (Cohen’s dz = 0.43), while the gap between adoption/career intention  and skills readiness was 0.418 points (dz = 0.74). In the structural model, reliability and relative  advantage significantly predicted skills readiness, while usefulness did not. Skills readiness  significantly predicted adoption/career intention (β = .202, p < .001), and usefulness and relative  advantage retained significant direct effects. Bootstrap mediation supported indirect effects for  reliability and relative advantage, but not usefulness. The findings indicate a readiness-to-capability  bottleneck: positive evaluations of AI-enabled networking do not automatically translate into perceived  capability to perform automation-related work. The paper contributes a context-sensitive model of  workforce readiness and offers implications for Cisco-oriented training, universities, employers and  national skills policy in Bangladesh.
